subject: Biotechnology
title: Whole Genome vs Exome Sequencing
description: One-minute skill: Whole Genome vs Exome Sequencing.

hook.text: The exome is only 1.5% of the genome — but contains 85% of disease-causing mutations. Why sequence the rest?

buildup.text: Exome sequencing captures only protein-coding regions — faster, cheaper, and easier to interpret than whole genome.

discovery.text: But regulatory regions, introns, and structural variants hide in the other 98.5% — the exome misses them.

twist.text: Non-coding variants cause diseases like pancreatic agenesis and limb malformations — the exome is not enough.

climax.text: As whole genome costs fall below exome costs, the debate is ending — sequence everything, analyze what you need.

punchline.text: Exome for speed, genome for completeness — costs decide the winner.

quiz.question: What is the main limitation of exome sequencing?
options: It cannot detect any genetic mutations
It misses non-coding variants, structural changes, and regulatory mutations in the other 98.5% of the genome
It is more expensive than whole genome sequencing

details.summary: Whole genome sequencing reads the entire 3 billion base pairs of human DNA, while whole exome sequencing targets only the 1 to 2 percent encoding proteins. WGS detects more variant types including structural and regulatory variants, but WES is cheaper and easier to interpret clinically.
details.whyItMatters: The choice between WGS and WES affects diagnostic yield, cost, and interpretability. As costs converge, WGS is becoming preferred for its comprehensive coverage, but clinical interpretation of non-coding variants remains challenging.
takeaways: WES covers protein-coding regions where most known disease mutations reside
WGS detects structural variants and non-coding variants that WES misses entirely
Diagnostic yield of WGS exceeds WES by 5 to 15 percent depending on the condition

faq.question: When is whole genome sequencing preferred over exome sequencing?
faq.answer: WGS is preferred when exome sequencing is negative in a patient with strong genetic suspicion, for conditions caused by structural variants or repeat expansions, when non-coding regulatory variants are suspected, and when comprehensive coverage is needed for the most complete analysis.

faq.question: Why is whole exome sequencing still commonly used if WGS is more comprehensive?
faq.answer: WES is cheaper, generates less data requiring less storage and computation, and focuses on regions where variant interpretation is most reliable. Over 85 percent of known disease-causing mutations are in coding regions. For many clinical scenarios, WES provides sufficient sensitivity at lower cost.
